title: Jericho
era_role: Closing rite of the Two EP. Jericho represents the oldest walled city on earth (11,000 years): just as its walls fell before sacred horns in Joshua 6, Vessel's psychological defenses crumble before the god's voice. Sleep feasts upon memories of former vessels ('Until I wake I dine on old encounters') while claiming new flesh.
in_character_quotes_gap_reason: Sleep Token granted very few interviews in 2016-2018 and never provided track-by-track in-character commentary.

editorial_reading.summary: Louder identifies Jericho as the earliest convergence of sensual R&B groove and heavy breakdowns: Vessel remains fixated on past attachments ('Until I wake I dine on old encounters'), declaring 'You taste like new flesh - say my name again'.
editorial_reading.source_title: Louder - The story behind every Sleep Token song

editorial_reading.summary: Cited as the world’s oldest walled city, Jericho has been inhabited for more than 11,000 years. The song that takes its name sees Vessel fixated on a previous relationship – possibly the one referenced in Nazareth. ‘Until I wake, I dine on old encounters,’ he intones. He seems to have moved on, though how that will play out isn’t clear. ‘You taste like new flesh – say my name again,’ he commands at one point. The quick bounce back and comparisons to past events suggest that, once again, it won’t last.
editorial_reading.source_title: Louder - The story behind every Sleep Token song (Page 1)

editorial_reading.summary: “Jericho”, considered to be the very first city in history, is also lyrically fitting for the beginning. Sleep appears to be searching for a new Vessel, and in the meantime he reminisces on experiences with previous Vessels (“Until I wake I dine on old encounters”), potentially in times when he was more powerful. Given the turbulent geopolitical history of the region, Jericho has seen the rise and fall of numerous civilizations – different populations, urban landscapes, religions – yet the city remained inhabited. New civilizations built over old ruins. This reflects many of the themes of Sundowning and TPWBYT, of the decay of the body and mind. The material dies, but the essence remains. Sleep remains.
editorial_reading.source_title: Boolin Tunes - The Lore of Sleep Token

editorial_reading.summary: Assuming that the Vessel of One, Two, Sundowning, and TPWBYT is the same, the record feels as though it documents him giving himself to Sleep and truly transitioning into ‘Vessel.’ Eternal reoccurrence appears an overarching paradigm of the band’s discography. “Jericho”, “Atlantic” (“Crumble like a temple built from future daughters to wasteland when the oceans recede” / “So flood me like Atlantic, weather me to nothing”), and “Fall For Me” (“In a city of ice there are burning cathedrals, turning the skies into glass”) refer to civilizational collapse as a metaphor for diachronic change. Relationships erode. Love fades. Happiness is in constant flux. Temples are typically the heart, even spirit, of civilizations. For that to simply crumble away to nothing necessitates decay, either internal or brought about by external intervention. “Temple built from future daughters” seems to yearn for a system of worship, in service of Sleep, whose constitution is eternal. Crumbling reiterates the band’s central tenet: nothing lasts forever.
editorial_reading.source_title: Boolin Tunes - The Lore of Sleep Token

references.category: religion / Old Testament (Joshua 6 & Book of Daniel)
references.detail: Dual biblical foundation: (1) the city of Jericho whose walls collapsed before sacred trumpets (Joshua 6), symbolizing Vessel's defenses collapsing before Sleep; (2) King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon ('Something in the way you lay / Enough to make the dead switch graves'), plagued by prophetic dreams in Daniel 2 and 4.
references.supporting_phrase: Say my name again... Until I wake, I'm yours

community_theories.theory: The reference to Nebuchadnezzar (the Babylonian king who lost his mind and was haunted by oneiric visions in Daniel 2 and 4) is cited by the community as proof that Vessel identifies with biblical monarchs humbled by an oneiric deity.
